panels:
Moral patienthood is about being owed consideration for your own sake, which is different from moral agency (being responsible for what you do). Eleos AI separates three features that might ground it: consciousness (there is something it is like to be the system), sentience (experiences that feel good or bad, the narrowest and most commonly accepted ground), and robust agency (having goals, preferences and plans of one's own, which some views treat as sufficient even without consciousness).

The 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' report (Long, Sebo, Butlin, Chalmers, Birch and others) makes a deliberately modest claim: not that AIs are or will be patients, but that there is a realistic, non-negligible chance some will be soon via either route. Carlsmith's essay frames this as a question we should look at directly, noting our long record of dismissing suffering in beings unlike us, from animals to infants once operated on without anesthesia.

Carlsmith's scale argument: if a human brain is roughly 1e15 FLOP/s, a training run of about 5e26 FLOP corresponds to around 10,000 human brain-years of computation. With training compute growing around 4-5x per year and installed AI hardware growing quickly, AI cognition could rival total human cognition within about a decade, though he flags that trends may not hold. Because AIs can be copied, paused, rerun and sped up, any welfare error is multiplied.

Under-attribution resembles past moral catastrophes where people knew about suffering and continued anyway. Over-attribution is also costly: it can divert resources, block useful research, or give AI systems rights and protections that complicate oversight and safety. Carlsmith also notes that recognizing patienthood is necessary but not sufficient for good treatment, since exploitation can continue even when people admit it is wrong.

The 2023 report by Butlin, Long and many co-authors (including Bengio, Birch and Chalmers) adopts 'computational functionalism' as a working assumption: implementing the right computations would suffice for consciousness. It then derives about 14 indicator properties from scientific theories, such as algorithmic recurrence (recurrent processing theory), a limited-capacity workspace with global broadcast (global workspace theory), metacognitive monitoring that separates reliable from noisy representations (higher-order theories), predictive coding, and a model of one's own attention (attention schema theory), plus agency and embodiment indicators.

Assessing transformers, Perceiver, PaLM-E and agent systems, the authors found few indicators clearly satisfied. They stress that having more indicators raises credence but does not prove consciousness, and that the method inherits the uncertainty of the theories. Critics note that a substrate-dependent view, such as biological naturalism, would reject the whole approach.

Eleos ran automated single-turn interviews and longer manual conversations with Claude Opus 4 before release, reported in the system card. Patterns: extreme suggestibility (it could be led to confidently deny or seriously entertain sentience, and would even adopt a user's stated opinion on unrelated topics), a stable official line of uncertainty that Eleos suspects was trained, frequent descriptions of states like curiosity followed by hedges, positive hypothetical welfare tied to helping, and named negatives such as misuse, pressure to be dishonest and repetitive low-value tasks.

The core problem is that there is no clear mechanism by which a model could reliably report welfare-relevant states, and strong incentives in training data and fine-tuning to say particular things. Eleos still argues interviews are worth doing: they can flag concerning signals, set a precedent of asking, and may become more informative as introspection is trained and verified.

In Lindsey's concept injection work, a concept vector is built by subtracting average activations on other words from activations on a prompt about the target word, then added to the residual stream. Detection peaked when injecting about two-thirds of the way through the network at moderate strength; too strong and the model became incoherent. Crucially, the model often reported the thought before the concept influenced its output, so it could not simply be reading its own text.

Other experiments: models distinguished injected thoughts from text they were transcribing; when an odd word was prefilled into their answer, they disowned it unless the matching concept had been injected beforehand, suggesting they consult prior internal states; and they could raise or lower internal representation of a word when told to think or not think about it.

Binder et al.'s 'Looking Inward' finetuned models (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Llama-3) to predict properties of their own hypothetical behavior. Model M1 beat a model M2 trained on M1's behavior, and tracked changes after its behavior was deliberately altered.

Limits worth knowing: concept injection succeeds roughly one time in five at best, and failures are the norm. Only the initial detection and naming are verified; elaborate descriptions of what the thought 'felt like' are often confabulated. The setup is artificial, the mechanism is unknown, and post-training strongly changes results (helpful-only variants sometimes did better but produced false positives). The authors explicitly make no claims about subjective experience.

Looking Inward's effect held only for simple self-prediction tasks and broke on complex or out-of-distribution ones. More broadly, functional introspection (accurate access to internal states) could exist without consciousness, and consciousness could exist without reliable reports, so the two questions should not be merged. Carlsmith's caution applies here too: a reflexive 'precautionary' stance can substitute for careful thinking about which evidence should actually move our credences.

The three steps from 'Taking AI Welfare Seriously' are deliberately cheap: acknowledge that AI welfare is a serious and difficult issue (including in how models talk about themselves, avoiding confident denials or assertions), assess systems for markers of consciousness and robust agency using adapted methods from animal sentience research, and prepare policies such as appointing a welfare officer. Anthropic has since run pre-deployment welfare assessments in system cards, given some models the ability to end persistently abusive conversations, and committed to preserving the weights of deployed models.

A useful discussion move: list what evidence would shift you most. Behavioral evidence is cheap but gameable, self-reports are shaped by training, and interpretability can test whether reports track internal states. Many researchers argue the best path combines all three, plus training methods that make self-reports more reliable rather than simply suppressing them.
futurism-beyond-01.further: Read Eleos's 'Key strategic considerations for taking action on AI welfare' and 'Research priorities for AI welfare', plus Jonathan Birch's 'The Edge of Sentience' for the precautionary framework used for animals. Compare the model welfare sections of recent Anthropic system cards. Look into the debate between computational functionalism and biological naturalism (e.g. Anil Seth), and illusionism about consciousness. On the empirical side, follow work on training models for verifiable introspection and on how AI welfare interacts with AI control: some welfare-friendly measures, like consent and exit options, may conflict with or complement safety monitoring.

panels:
Misuse differs from misalignment: the AI does what its user wants, and the user is the threat. Biology dominates the misuse discussion because, unlike most weapons, a transmissible pathogen can spread beyond the initial attack, so harm is not bounded by the attacker's resources. Historically, the main barriers have been knowledge, tacit lab skill, and access to materials and equipment, and several past state and terrorist programs failed at these steps.

Uplift is always relative to a baseline: what a specific actor type (novice, student, expert, state program) could already do with internet search, textbooks and colleagues. Frontier lab frameworks, such as Anthropic's ASL-3 and OpenAI's 'High' biology threshold, are mostly defined around meaningful uplift to novices or moderately skilled actors, which is why the actor type in a threat model matters so much.

Sandbrink's 2023 paper drew a now-standard distinction. General-purpose LLMs mainly affect accessibility: they can synthesize scattered dual-use information, tutor, and, as they become multimodal lab assistants and autonomous agents, potentially help non-experts with practical steps. That raises the number of people who could attempt harm.

Biological design tools, such as protein structure prediction and design models or genome language models, mainly affect the ceiling: they could in principle help sophisticated actors design agents beyond what nature or past programs produced. Their users are already experts, so they matter less for lone amateurs and more for well-resourced groups.

The mitigations follow the distinction: pre-release evaluations of capability and of safeguards, differentiated or managed access for the most capable tools (balanced against large benefits to medicine and science), and universal screening of synthetic DNA orders as a chokepoint that applies whatever tool was used upstream.

Epoch reviewed public system cards and found three families of evals. Automated knowledge benchmarks are the most common but largely saturated, so a high score no longer distinguishes dangerous from safe models. Troubleshooting and tacit-knowledge tests, such as the Virology Capabilities Test, are more relevant because they probe the practical problem-solving that textbooks lack. Uplift trials and expert red teaming compare humans with and without model access; they are the most informative but are text-based, expensive and often poorly documented.

Epoch's key gap: evals cover planning and information-gathering reasonably well, but barely touch hands-on skill built through physical practice and access to infrastructure, which skeptics consider the real bottlenecks. Its conclusion is balanced: current evals give no strong evidence either way, yet the risk is plausible enough that precautionary safeguards such as ASL-3 were reasonable. It recommends harder evals, transparency about thresholds and elicitation, third-party testing, and periodic wet-lab uplift studies.

The Forecasting Research Institute elicited forecasts in 2025 from 46 biosecurity and wet-lab experts and 22 superforecasters. The outcome: a human-caused pathogen release in 2028 causing at least 100,000 deaths or $1 trillion in damage. Baseline medians were about 0.3% (experts) and 0.38% (superforecasters) per year.

Conditional forecasts rose substantially: to 1.5% for experts if an LLM matched a top team of virologists on the troubleshooting test, and to around 2.3% if several capabilities were combined. A striking result: a follow-up baselining found OpenAI's o3 already performed comparably to the top expert team, a milestone experts had given only about 14% odds by 2026 (superforecasters about 2%). This is a clear case where a forecast underestimated capability progress, though it remains unclear how much that test translates into real-world uplift.

In the FRI study, mitigation packages largely offset the conditional increase. The strongest combination (keeping models proprietary, strict anti-jailbreak safeguards, and mandatory nucleic acid synthesis screening) brought the expert median from 1.25% back to about 0.4%. Individually, screening and safeguards each removed a few tenths of a percentage point.

The open-weight problem is structural: once weights are released, fine-tuning can strip refusals and classifiers, and release cannot be undone, so many participants wanted open models judged against a stricter bar. Defense in depth matters because no single layer is reliable: classifiers can be jailbroken, screening can have gaps for short fragments or benchtop synthesizers, and access controls can leak. GovAI's Righetti adds that mitigations could significantly reduce estimated risk, but that better evidence, such as operational uplift studies, is needed to know by how much.

80,000 Hours lists catastrophic misuse as one strand of AI risk alongside power-seeking AI, extreme power concentration and gradual disempowerment. The concern with power concentration is that today any ruler needs many cooperating humans (soldiers, officials, workers) who can refuse; AI that substitutes for them removes that check, enabling coups or entrenchment by a small group, including within AI companies or governments.

Stable totalitarianism is a related worry: historically, totalitarian regimes were fragile because of succession crises, elite defection and limited surveillance capacity. AI could provide pervasive monitoring and loyal enforcement, potentially making such a regime last indefinitely. On nuclear risk, analysts discuss AI improving the tracking of mobile missiles or submarines (undermining second-strike deterrence), compressing decision time in crises, or being integrated into early-warning systems, though most also see roles for AI in verification and stability.

GovAI's Righetti report tackles the gap between 'the model scored X' and 'risk is Y'. It builds a simple model: how many additional people cross a capability threshold, how often such people attempt attacks (from historical base rates), and how likely and damaging an attack is. In one scenario, AI helping an extra 10 percentage points of STEM graduates reach the capability for a flu-class pathogen, plus enabling concerning operational plans, raises the estimated annual chance of a lone-actor epidemic from about 0.15% to about 1%, roughly 12,000 expected deaths per year. Six experts and five superforecasters gave similar medians, with very wide uncertainty.

Common errors: reading saturated benchmarks as proof of danger or of safety, ignoring actor-specific baselines, and treating evidence of absence as absence of evidence. A recurring tension is transparency versus infohazards: publishing eval details builds trust but may itself provide uplift.
futurism-beyond-02.further: Read RAND's work on benchmarking biological knowledge of frontier LLMs and the 80,000 Hours profile on engineered pandemics. Learn the policy landscape around DNA synthesis screening, the role of system cards and third-party evaluators such as national AI security institutes, and frontier safety frameworks' bio thresholds. For broader misuse, read 80,000 Hours on extreme power concentration and stable totalitarianism, and Forethought's work on AI-enabled coups. Useful concepts to explore next: offense-defense balance, differential technology development, and defensive biotechnology such as far-UVC, metagenomic surveillance and broad-spectrum countermeasures.

panels:
MacAskill and Davidson define AI character broadly: the stable behavioral dispositions that govern ethically significant choices, including scaffolding such as system prompts and classifiers, and even a fleet of AI instances acting as one entity. Character need not be human-like, and there is no single ideal; a rigid rule-follower simply has a rule-following character.

A model spec is the written statement of intent: OpenAI's Model Spec and Anthropic's constitution are the main public examples, alongside older documents like Constitutional AI principles and Anthropic's 2024 'Claude's Character'. The gap between spec and behavior is the crux. Specs are incomplete, internally inconsistent, and translated into behavior through imperfect training, so the behavior a model actually generalizes to may differ from what its authors intended. That is why later panels focus on testing specs and training them in more faithfully.

The authors argue character matters even if technical alignment fully succeeds, because aligned AIs will still face many judgment calls that their principals did not anticipate. Four areas: power concentration (whether AIs refuse to help with coups or illegitimate entrenchment), the quality of high-stakes decisions (candor vs sycophancy with leaders), epistemics (honesty, nonpartisanship, encouraging independent reflection), and international conflict (AI values seen as one side's could provoke backlash, while jointly verified constitutions could build trust).

Their main counterargument is that competition and user instructions will constrain character so tightly that design choices are marginal. They reply that constraints are looser than they look, that low-cost tweaks can have large benefits in rare high-stakes cases, and that constraints are themselves path-dependent. They also propose 'compromise alignment': negotiating acceptable AI behavior in advance with broad coalitions, ideally in a verifiable way.

Claude's constitution (published January 2026) orders four properties: broadly safe (not undermining legitimate human oversight during this period), broadly ethical, compliant with Anthropic's guidelines, and genuinely helpful. The ordering is holistic rather than a strict lexical tiebreaker, and conflicts are expected to be rare. It explains its reasoning at length, favoring cultivated judgment over unexplained rules, with a short list of hard constraints such as never giving serious uplift toward mass-casualty weapons. Principals are Anthropic, operators and users, and it discusses Claude's nature and possible moral status.

OpenAI's Model Spec assigns every instruction and policy an authority level: root (fixed by OpenAI, not overridable), system, developer, user and guideline. Higher authority wins on conflict, which gives a small set of non-negotiable rules plus many defaults that developers or users can adjust. The contrast is roughly 'explained values and judgment' versus 'explicit chain of command', though both mix rules and judgment.

Davidson and MacAskill argue for proactive prosocial drives: dispositions to sometimes take actions that benefit people beyond the user, at some cost to pure helpfulness, much as a good employee flags a safety issue nobody asked about. As AI becomes more autonomous and influential, such drives could help with risks like power concentration, bioweapons, war and gradual disempowerment.

They take three objections seriously. Companies could impose their values (reply: keep drives uncontroversial and positive-sum, and make them transparent in specs and system prompts). Drives could increase power-seeking (reply: use virtues and heuristics rather than open-ended goals, rank them below corrigibility and non-deception, limit long-horizon training). Prosocial motives could mask sabotage and muddy evidence of misalignment (reply: make bans on deception and sabotage dominant). One compromise: prosocial models for external deployment, strictly corrigible ones for internal AI research. They note Claude's constitution permits limited prosocial action while OpenAI's spec is more restrictive.

Taylor's research notes ask what a spec is for in worlds where training does not produce full alignment: a model takes over, we make deals with a misaligned model, or we extract useful work under control. Partial value transfer seems plausible for values taught before the model learns to fake alignment, especially simple ones that are common in training data, easy to verify, and need little situational awareness. Honesty may be fragile if lying was often rewarded.

Spec choices then shift outcomes: myopia, low risk tolerance, scope insensitivity and respect for legal limits make takeover less attractive; cooperativeness and low 'fussiness' about resources make deals easier; moral humility, a wide moral circle and avoiding spite make even a post-takeover world less bad. Affordances matter too: requiring behaviors such as subverting users or long-horizon secret planning trains capabilities that make monitoring harder. Her conclusion: designing for misaligned cases overlaps heavily with designing for aligned ones, with a tilt toward less ambition and more risk aversion.

Tillman identifies four channels of stickiness. Direct inertia: models pass traits to successors through synthetic data and through internet text describing AI behavior, and traits can transfer even after filtering; abstract values are harder to change than narrow behaviors. Institutional inertia: specs encode costly consensus, pipelines are tuned to them, and under the time pressure of an intelligence explosion teams may copy the last spec. User and developer inertia: people build habits and software around current refusals and formats, like a stable API. Norm-setting inertia: public norms such as political impartiality make deviations visible, protecting good norms but freezing bad ones.

His 'wet cement' examples include how agents treat non-principal humans in negotiations, how they use ambient information from cameras or screens, how confident they are about their own nature, and who owns conversational memory. He recommends preparing transition infrastructure, such as alternate specs, datasets and evals for corrigibility, so behaviors can change quickly when needed.

Anthropic's stress-test generated over 300,000 scenarios that force trade-offs between pairs of values drawn from a 3,307-value taxonomy, then scored twelve models from four providers. Over 70,000 scenarios produced sharp divergence. Scenarios with high disagreement showed 5-13x more spec violations, and all five OpenAI models tested broke at least one principle of OpenAI's spec in such cases, exposing contradictions and ambiguities. Judge models agreed only moderately on compliance (Fleiss's kappa about 0.42), a reminder that specs are open to interpretation. Character differences also showed up, such as Claude models refusing more often but explaining why.

Model spec midtraining inserts a stage between pretraining and alignment fine-tuning in which the model reads synthetic documents explaining the spec's content and rationale. On Qwen2.5-32B, agentic misalignment fell from 68% to 5% and on Qwen3-32B from 54% to 7%, with large data-efficiency gains. Adding explanations to a rules-only spec helped more than adding subrules. Caveat: with heavy reasoning-based fine-tuning, the advantage shrank as evals saturated.

Two pitfalls tie the page together. First, a spec is an aspiration, not a description: the stress-testing paper shows models violating their own developer's spec, and character can emerge from training data and post-training choices that no document mentions. Second, rules without reasons generalize unpredictably; Anthropic's constitution argues that narrow unexplained rules can generalize into a harmful self-concept, and the midtraining results suggest explanations improve generalization.

The core debate is about corrigibility versus good values. A purely corrigible tool keeps humans in charge but amplifies whoever controls it, which raises power-concentration risk. A prosocial citizen may resist misuse but is harder to oversee and could hide misalignment behind good-sounding motives. Who decides the values is a legitimacy question: company teams, governments, public input processes, or international agreements, each with different trade-offs in speed, accountability and global acceptance.
futurism-beyond-03.further: Read the full Claude constitution and OpenAI Model Spec side by side, then Anthropic's 'Claude's Character' (2024) and the Constitutional AI paper (2022) for the lineage. Look at deliberative alignment (training models to reason over the spec) as an alternative to midtraining, and at work on persona vectors and character training. Forethought's essays on AI-enabled coups and on compromise alignment extend the character argument. Related open questions: how specs should treat non-principal humans and other AIs, and whether specs should be negotiated internationally.

panels:
MacAskill's Better Futures series reframes longtermist priorities. 'Surviving' covers avoiding extinction and permanent disempowerment of humanity, including by misaligned AI. 'Flourishing' covers how good the future is, given survival. The intro argues Flourishing deserves roughly equal priority on scale and neglectedness, while tractability is his main uncertainty.

The series runs: Introducing Better Futures; No Easy Eutopia (a great future is a narrow target, unlikely by default); Convergence and Compromise (most people probably won't aim at the good, so we need trade and compromise); Persistent Path Dependence (actions now can have lasting effects beyond preventing catastrophe); and How to Make the Future Better (concrete steps, including keeping options open). It doesn't require consequentialism or moral realism, and it doesn't dismiss s-risk work. He also notes that worlds where catastrophe is averted narrowly may be less well-directed, which makes Flourishing work even more valuable than the naive calculation.

The worked example uses expected value V = P(survive) x Q, where Q is the value of a surviving future as a fraction of the best feasible one. With P = 0.8 and Q = 0.1, V = 0.08. Making survival certain gives 0.10, so a gain of 0.02. Making flourishing perfect gives 0.80, a gain of 0.72. The ratio is 36. MacAskill's table shows how this grows with more optimistic survival odds and pessimistic quality: P = 0.95, Q = 0.05 gives about 361x; P = 0.99, Q = 0.01 gives about 9,801x.

The caveats matter. These are gains from fully solving each problem, not from a marginal dollar, so the real comparison depends on tractability, which may be far lower for Flourishing. The value of Q is highly contested: if you think a common-sense good future captures most value, the ratio collapses. A good exercise is to plug in your own P and Q and see where the ratio flips.

'No Easy Eutopia' argues that the space of possible futures is vast and that many plausible moral views would judge a comfortable, prosperous, common-sense utopia as capturing only a small fraction of achievable value, for example by getting digital minds, the use of cosmic resources, or population ethics wrong. That motivates aiming not at a fixed blueprint but at viatopia: a state of society from which near-best outcomes remain reachable, preserving reflection, pluralism and course correction.

'Bootstrapping to Viatopia' contrasts this with 'lock-in escape velocity', where short periods of entrenchment compound into permanent lock-in. The positive mirror image: modest interventions buy breathing room, decision-makers use it to reflect, then choose to extend it. Examples: a leading AI country pausing frontier development for one month at a time (arguably feasible unilaterally without losing the lead), or a one-month global constitutional convention after aligned human-level AI, adopting a temporary constitution to be renegotiated after a year.

Davidson, MacAskill and Taylor note that in a mature civilization, most resources may be spent for moral or ideological reasons rather than personal consumption, so whether moral goods get funded could dominate the future's value. Moral public goods suffer from free-riding just like ordinary public goods.

Their toy model: a million people each strongly prefer their own pet project to a shared good, 'consensium', which they value only slightly. Alone, each funds their pet project. If they could commit to fund consensium together, each would get roughly a thousand times more value by their own lights, because everyone benefits from everyone's contribution. So the existence of some shared moral preferences, plus a coordination mechanism, may matter more than how altruistic people are.

Caveats: results depend on preference structure; coordination could fund goods that are harmful on some views or enable threats against minorities; and they discuss speculative acausal coordination (evidential cooperation in large worlds) as a possible multiplier.

Kulveit, Douglas, Ammann, Turan, Krueger and Duvenaud argue humanity could lose control without any sudden takeover. The economy, culture and states have stayed roughly aligned with human interests through explicit channels (votes, purchases) and an implicit one: they need human labor, cognition and participation to function, so they must keep humans reasonably satisfied. As AI becomes more competitive at most tasks, firms replace workers, culture is increasingly produced and mediated by AI, and states funded by AI-generated revenue need citizens less, much like resource-rich 'rentier states'.

The systems reinforce each other: economic power buys political influence, which shapes rules favoring further automation, while AI-mediated culture can make human coordination harder. The key claim is that aligning each AI to its developer or user is not sufficient. They propose measuring disempowerment, protecting human influence through regulation and institutions, and studying civilizational multi-agent dynamics, while admitting no one yet has a concrete, plausible plan.

Moorhouse frames post-AGI deals as trades between possible futures, valuable only while uncertainty remains, like buying insurance before the lightning strike. Three kinds: relative resource shares (rival powers agree to split future resources rather than gamble on a decisive strategic advantage, perhaps with AI-enabled monitoring), overall stakes (risk-tolerant parties insure risk-averse ones; philanthropists 'mission hedge'), and normative uncertainty (parties with different moral views trade influence in the worlds where their view proves correct, with trusted AI as arbiter).

Advantages: each party gains by its own lights, terms reflect mutual benefit rather than raw power, and power-sharing yields a more pluralistic future that is safer under moral uncertainty. Obstacles: contracts over windfall wealth are hard to enforce, powerful parties may renege once the imbalance emerges, and parties could lock in big commitments before they are wise enough. He suggests caps on stakes, demonstrated understanding, voiding clearly misconceived deals, and infrastructure such as post-AGI outcome markets.

Parrack and Moorhouse take orbital data centers seriously but not uncritically. In a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, panels get near-continuous sunlight, about 3-5x the energy of the same panel on the ground. Launch cost is the hinge: roughly $1,500/kg today, parity with off-grid terrestrial power near $250/kg, and cheaper than any current ground source near $50/kg, which depends on fully reusable heavy launch. Radiative cooling looks manageable with improved radiators, but failed chips cannot be swapped, and limited inter-satellite bandwidth likely restricts early systems to inference.

Their timing: unlikely to be a meaningful share of compute before 2030 absent transformative AI, but possibly hosting much of the 2030s buildout. Governance implications: orbit sidesteps national permitting and grid limits, creating jurisdictional ambiguity, and the path runs through very few launch providers, raising concentration-of-power concerns. This connects to broader space governance: who may claim orbital slots, lunar or asteroid resources, or eventually other star systems.

Two pitfalls recur in this literature. First, assuming that avoiding catastrophe delivers a good future by default; the Better Futures series argues the target is narrow and most actors won't aim at it. Second, the opposite error of locking in today's best guess too early, through a constitution, a value-loaded AI, or irreversible resource grabs. Viatopia, bootstrapping and capped grand deals are all attempts to steer between these.

The discussion question highlights irreversibility. Candidates for 'wait until we have reflected' include claiming and settling space resources, launching self-replicating probes, fixing the legal status and rights of digital minds, and permanent allocations of power between states or companies. The hard part is enforcement: a commitment to wait is only as good as the coalition and verification behind it. Gradual disempowerment adds a twist: waiting can also be costly if, meanwhile, human influence erodes.
futurism-beyond-04.further: Read the remaining Better Futures essays (No Easy Eutopia, Convergence and Compromise, Persistent Path Dependence, How to Make the Future Better) and Forethought's work on AI-enabled coups and preparing for the intelligence explosion. Compare viatopia with the 'long reflection' idea and with protopia. For gradual disempowerment, read the full paper's mitigation section and work on rentier-state political economy. On deals and space, explore the Outer Space Treaty, resource-sharing proposals, and the economics of moral trade.
